title: Vesicular Protocells at the Origin of Life: A Critical Review and a Bounded Bio-Inspired Analogy
content: Membrane-bounded vesicles assembled from prebiotically plausible amphiphiles remain one of the most experimentally supported models of early compartmentalization. Mixed single-chain amphiphiles form vesicles over a wider pH and salinity range than early single-component fatty-acid systems; such vesicles can grow, divide by physically or chemically simple routes, and, in selected formulations, host limited nonenzymatic nucleic-acid chemistry. This article reviews those results, with emphasis on work since the 2018 syntheses of Joyce and Szostak and of Chen and Walde, and separates them from a second, independent question: whether modern microbial biofilms can be used as functional analogs when thinking about matrix-stabilized compartments.The two questions are independent in claim-type and must not be fused, but they are linked by an explicit translation rule. Extracellular polymeric substances, short-chain fatty acids, and other products of evolved metabolism are not demonstrated prebiotic building blocks. A publicly posted preprint by the present author coupled a vesicular framework to microbial-biofilm language [20]. Preliminary morphological observations of heat-treated probiotic biofilms after rehydration, developed in drafts leading to that preprint, do not establish a vesicle-to-cell transition, do not document sterility, and cannot be read as abiogenesis. Even a later, well-controlled demonstration of survival after autoclaving would concern persistence of pre-existing biological material, not the emergence of cells from nonliving chemistry. An informal coupling of pH gradients to zeta potential is retained only as a qualitative analogy that currently lacks defined variables, energy accounting, kinetics, and falsifying predictions.The recommended path is therefore split in its inferences and joined in its constraints: a microbiological study of matrix-protected survival, if pursued at all, should meet sterilization-validation standards and remain silent on origin-of-life claims; protocell experiments should start from abiotic amphiphile mixtures and specified geochemical boundary conditions, and should obey the same translation rules used to reject the biofilm reading. Within those limits, vesicular models continue to offer a coherent experimental program for the chemistry-to-biology transition.
